#966. Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

Evidence suggests exercise can keep more cancer patients alive. But what does "living longer" actually mean, and who does it apply to?

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.   In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.

#965. Whiff of arrogance as Arsenal unexpectedly implode

Arsenal were cruising. This was life on Premier League easy street, but from complete control of this game against Newcastle United, they tossed it away. It was a spectacular, unexpected implosion. They were extremely fortunate to escape with a point.

You cannot switch off away from home in the Premier League and you certainly can never be complacent against a team with Newcastle’s home crowd behind them.

From control to disarray. From looking like champions, Arsenal, who also lost goalkeeper David Raya to a worrying looking injury, rumbled under pressure. To go from dominance to being grateful for a draw, this was a flaky side of the Premier League leaders we have not seen for a while.

“We have lost two points,” said manager Mikel Arteta. “We were exceptional in the first half, the intensity and the quality, we should have been two, three or four goals up.

“When you don’t do that, in the second half you cannot give the opposition belief and you cannot give them goals. We did both. We started to lose duels, second balls, we gave it away.”

Was it arrogance? Did the title-holders start to believe they were simply too good to be hurt or worried by a team with Newcastle’s obvious limitations? It looked like it. The way Arsenal fell apart as soon as the momentum in the game shifted in the home team’s favour in the second half was shocking.

Newcastle were dreadful before the break and managed just one attack before half-time. Perhaps it was all too easy for Arteta’s side. They have become used to ferocious battles on Tyneside, but this was a stroll for 45 minutes. When it turned into a proper test after half-time, though, they folded.

"Absolutely clinical!" Eberechi Eze scores his first Premier League goal of the season to give Arsenal the lead 🔴 https://t.co/34IbZuuJuN

The visitors took a deserved lead, through Eberechi Eze, having barely had to break sweat, but the way they approached the second half was baffling. As soon as Newcastle got in their faces and made it a scrap, Arsenal were bullied, ruffled and rushed into mistakes.

To give the opposition one goal against the run of play can be forgiven, but to do it a second time, when the heat is cranked up, hints at a fragility we no longer thought existed under Arteta.

The first goal came from a blunder by captain Martin Odegaard. It was a lazy, sloppy swing of the leg to try to clear a throw-in and the ball sliced backwards. When it looped into the path of Will Osula, he squared to the unmarked Harvey Barnes who put away the equaliser comfortably.

"Horrendous error!" Harvey Barnes puts Newcastle level 👊 https://t.co/YWrHZPxBIo

It was Newcastle’s first shot on target, but Arsenal’s air of invincibility vanished and the crowd sensed it. Newcastle players responded to the noise, snapping into tackles and pouring forward in numbers, yet the second goal was also an Arsenal gift.

How do you leave the giant Dan Burn unmarked at a corner? Newcastle’s captain had so much time and space the crowd were able to scream in anticipation before his header flew goalwards, eventually bundled across the line by his centre-back colleague Malick Thiaw.

Malick Thiaw is in the right place to fire it in and give Newcastle the lead against Arsenal! 🔥 https://t.co/nthaH3aOJD

Newcastle deserved it. For half an hour in the second half they were the better side. From the depths of despair, from the apathy and boos of half-time, this was a completely different team.

If this is the vertical football Matthias Jaissle has preached since he arrived in August, Newcastle supporters can buy into it. There was speed, a physicality and a boldness in this second-half performance. It was fun and exciting. It was football played on the front foot. It was what we were promised when the German replaced Eddie Howe.

“That is Newcastle’s DNA, the second half is what we want this team to play like,” said Jaissle. “We knew there would be ups and downs this season, but if we can put that performance together for 90 minutes we can definitely say we are moving in the right direction.”

The problem is, Newcastle have not put a 90-minute performance like this together all season. We have only seen it in flashes and as good as the second half was, we cannot lose sight of the fact the first was abject. Newcastle’s football was aimless, clueless and dysfunctional. One attack before the break, one deflected shot wide is simply not good enough.

The transformation at half-time was unexpected. The substitutes helped; Tino Livramento was a massive upgrade on Amar Dedic at right-back, Jacob Ramsey improved the midfield and Anthony Elanga brought speed and, yes, a vertical threat to their attack.

But Jaissle’s side did not hold on for the win. They had the chances to score a third, but it was their ambition to do so that caused their downfall. Arsenal’s class shone again, passing through the lines to release Noni Madueke.

The winger still had lots to do, but having cut inside, leaving two Newcastle defenders on the ground, his shot squeezed through a crowd and through the arms of goalkeeper Lukasz Hornicek. The Czech international will not want to see it again, and this comes after a similar mistake in the home defeat to Everton.

Noni Madueke equalises for Arsenal! 💥 https://t.co/VNXOoNDxiJ

Speaking to Sky Sports, the Arsenal boss said: “My feeling is that we lost two points today. I think we were exceptional in the first half. At every level. Our intensity, the clarity that we have, how to attack the jumps of Newcastle every time they wanted to go man-to-man, the composure that we have, the way we use our relationship to break their press. And it should have been 2-0, 3-0 or 4-0 up, clear.

“But it wasn’t. And when it wasn’t, then we expected in the second half that we have to again raise the level because the opponent is going to have a reaction. And the opponent did have a reaction and we were very below the level that is required to stretch the gap in a game like this in this stadium. And then we gave them belief.

“And I say we give them belief because we give them a goal, we give them a throw-in that we just give them the ball. We have no structure to control the opposite winger. We concede a goal and it’s game on. And from that it became a very chaotic game. Every set-piece, we know that they are exceptional at it and we concede from a set piece.

“And then you have to react. And then we went back to the team that the exceptional team that we were in the first half again for another 25 minutes and we scored a great goal. We create infinity of openings to create and score the third goal, but we lack some time or to be precise, to make that count.”

A brave second-half display earns Newcastle a well-deserved draw against Arsenal. After falling behind to Eze’s 33rd-minute opener, Jaissle made a triple change at the break that completely transformed the hosts, who scored twice through Barnes and Thiaw. However, Arsenal fought back and levelled thanks to Madueke as both sides had to settle for a draw. Arsenal drop points for just the second time in 11 league matches this season and stay top, while Newcastle remain 12th.

It finishes level at St. James' Park 🤝 https://t.co/jwFfknJKxh

Gyokeres darts inside of Livramento to work a yard of space, but whips a powerful effort over the bar. He claims Arsenal should have a corner, but the referee rules that it’s a goal kick. Time is rapidly running out for both sides to score a late winner.

Arteta is searching for a hero and orders a late double attacking change in stoppage time. Merino and Gyokeres are on for Havertz and Odegaard.

Hall was at fault for Arsenal’s opener but has been brilliant in the second half. He slumps to the deck and hobbles off for Botman. It’s unclear whether it’s an injury or fatigue. Newcastle fans will pray it is the latter.

There will be nine minutes of added time. More drama is a definite possibility.

Arsenal are on top and piling the pressure on Newcastle as we approach the 90-minute mark. The hosts deserve something from this game based on their second-half display.

It’s end-to-end action at the moment, with both teams looking shaky at the back. It would not be at all surprising if either side found another goal.

Newcastle make a late attacking change as Wissa replaces Willock. Can he help his side find a late winner?

Burn catches Timber with a late, sliding tackle in the corner as the Arsenal man goes to cross. The Newcastle captain tells Timber to get up and Madueke rushes over to defend his teammate before he and Burn start pushing each other. Both players are carded for that flashpoint and Arsenal take a free kick, which Hornicek catches comfortably.

It’s brilliant build-up from the league leaders. Havertz and Odegaard combine, with the latter playing in Madueke. The Arsenal winger cuts inside a couple of desperate Newcastle challengers before squeezing a slightly deflected effort underneath Hornicek. The Newcastle goalkeeper should probably do better, but Arsenal have responded like champions. This game is so finely poised now.

Noni Madueke equalises for Arsenal! 💥 https://t.co/VNXOoNDxiJ

Miley darts into Arsenal’s penalty area after receiving Barnes’ pass. For a split-second, it looked like Rice was about to commit a last-man foul as he weighed up whether to pull Miley down, but Kepa rushes out to intercept and save his side on this occasion.

Newcastle fly forward again as Willock’s strong run and deflected shot earns the hosts a corner. From Hall’s delivery, Havertz inadvertently flicks the ball against his own crossbar. It’s wave after wave of Newcastle pressure.

Nobody saw this coming at half time. Arsenal were cruising and in complete control but they gifted Newcastle an equaliser through Martin Ødegaard’s sliced clearance and something stirred inside St James’ Park. The atmosphere completely shifted and the champions have wilted under a sudden wave of Newcastle pressure. Complacency is dangerous especially away at Newcastle. You do not leave Dan Burn unmarked at a corner. Arsenal have self destructed.

Confirmation of that triple change for Arsenal as Kepa, Lewis-Skelly and Tzolis replace Raya, Guimaraes and Eze. Unsurprisingly, Guimaraes was heavily booed as he departed.

Raya looks to be in serious discomfort and can’t continue as he walks off holding his arm. Kepa is ready to come on. This second half has been a disaster for Arsenal. It also looks like Tzolis and Lewis-Skelly are coming on.

Newcastle look like a completely different side in this second half. Credit to Jaissle, his triple half-time change has worked wonders. Surely Arteta must be considering some substitutions of his own soon. Raya is down again and seems to have an issue with his shoulder or arm.

Incredible scenes! No one saw this coming at half-time. Hall curls in a corner and Burn peels away from Timber at the back post. Raya does well to save the Newcastle captain’s unmarked header, but Thiaw reacts quickest to knock in the rebound from close range. The home players rush to the corner to celebrate in front of the jubilant Gallowgate End. The goal survives a VAR check and Newcastle’s lead is confirmed. What are Arsenal made of now?

Malick Thiaw is in the right place to fire it in and give Newcastle the lead against Arsenal! 🔥 https://t.co/nthaH3aOJD

Miley tries his luck from long range and arrows a strike at goal which is straight at Raya. It stings the palms of the Arsenal goalkeeper. Yet again, it’s another positive moment for Newcastle.

This game is getting more feisty as Barnes catches Konsa with the hosts springing a high press. The Newcastle goal-scorer is booked for the challenge.

Hall dispossesses Madueke and gallops down the wing. Rice can’t catch him and bumps into the back of the defender to earn himself a yellow card. Arsenal look slighly rattled in this second half.

All of a sudden, Newcastle have seized the initiative and are taking the game to Arsenal. Osula nearly latches onto Barnes’ knock-down at the back post as he beats Timber to a cross, but Raya is alert and catches the ball.

Where did that come from?! Out of nowhere, Newcastle are level. It’s a dreadful error from Odegaard, who wildly swings his boot at a throw-in. The Arsenal captain doesn’t clear or control it, allowing Osula to thread a pass into Barnes. The winger then slides a clever effort into the bottom corner to beat Raya and the hosts are back on terms. St James’ Park has woken up now.

"Horrendous error!" Harvey Barnes puts Newcastle level 👊 https://t.co/YWrHZPxBIo

Raya is back on his feet and is okay to continue. Kepa was briefly warming up on the sidelines but it looks like he won’t be needed.

We are back under way for the second half.

Jaissle has ordered a triple change, with Ramsey, Elanga and Livramento replacing Steur, Murphy and Dedic.

There’s a break in the play at the start of this half as Willock accidentally collides with Raya and the Arsenal goalkeeper holds his head. The medical staff are on to treat him.

Another abject, clueless, and directionless performance from Newcastle United in front of their own supporters. Arsenal have dominated the game and have not had to get out of second gear. It is hard to see what Matthias Jaissle’s team is trying to do and patience is wearing thin.

Yes, of course, they are playing the best team in the country but the supporters are not stupid. They have seen this sort of performance far too many times already this season. The most damning thing you can say is that there is no excitement. Even the boos for Bruno are half-hearted.

Boos ring out on the half-time whistle from the home fans. It’s been complete and utter domination from Arsenal. Eze’s resounding finish separates the sides, but the visitors could easily be two or three goals ahead. Newcastle look clueless in possession and are yet to record a shot on target.

Hall makes a goal-saving block! On this occasion, he comes to Newcastle’s rescue. Odegaard rolls a pass into the onrushing Madueke, who makes a great run drifting in from the right wing. Hall tracks the Arsenal attacker and makes a brilliant sliding block to deny Madueke from close range.

Once again, Hall switches off and Madueke pounces on the defender’s mistake as he tries to let the ball travel out of play. Madueke keeps it in and leads an Arsenal attack, but from a tight angle and under pressure from the covering Thiaw, his shot is smothered by Hornicek.

Arsenal are cruising and we’re still waiting for Newcastle to wake up. The away side haven’t created loads of chances, but they’re in control and have limited the hosts to nearly zero attacking threat.

After zero goals in his first ten matches for club and country this season, Eberechi Eze has now scored three goals in his last eight appearances.

All the noise inside St James’ Park is coming from the travelling Arsenal fans. Newcastle look lost and are really struggling to fashion any patterns of play in possession.

It’s a clinical opener for the visitors and Eze has his first Premier League goal of the season. Hall fails to deal with Konsa’s long ball and Havertz steals possession from him. The German then slides a delightful reverse pass behind Dedic and through to Eze, who lets the ball run across his body before smashing a clinical one-on-one effort into the roof of the net. Arsenal are deservedly ahead and Newcastle have barely laid a glove on them.

"Absolutely clinical!" Eberechi Eze scores his first Premier League goal of the season to give Arsenal the lead 🔴 https://t.co/34IbZuuJuN

St James’ Park was about to erupt, and not in a good way for the hosts! Rice clips such an inviting cross into the box and Guimaraes throws himself at the delivery, directing it narrowly wide of the bottom corner with an outstretched leg. The Newcastle fans behind the goal give the Brazilian some stick as he gets back to his feet.

Arsenal are dominating possession and territory. Newcastle United are struggling to advance up the pitch, and once again, there still seems to be no real improvement in Jaissle’s “vertical football” approach.

The theory following the German’s move from Saudi Arabia was that his team is better suited to playing against stronger opponents when there are more gaps to exploit in a side that constantly looks to attack.

We shall see about that. Other than a deflected Jacob Murphy shot from distance the home team has not had a meaningful attack yet.

Dedic picks up the game’s first yellow card after he pulls Eze back. The Newcastle right-back needs to be careful now.

After 23 minutes, Newcastle goalkeeper Lukás Hornícek has had 15 touches of the ball. Only Dan Burn and Lewis Hall have had more for Newcastle. The home side seem unable to work the ball forward at all. Seemingly every passage of possession results in a Newcastle player turning towards their own goal and shovelling it back to the keeper.

Safe to say that Hornicek does not look comfortable with the ball at his feet. Dedic passes back to him and under a little bit of pressure from Odegaard, he boots the ball straight out of play. From there, Arsenal fashion an attack as Timber strides forward and finds Havertz, who lashes a shot wide from a tight angle.

This game is yet to burst into life. It’s been a relatively measured start from both sides so far. Guimaraes has only had 12 touches so the boos have been limited to this point.

Murphy chops inside of Calafiori and smashes a shot at goal. It takes a massive deflection off Barnes, who was trying to get out of the way, but the ball flies just wide of Arsenal’s near post. Raya was worried for a second there as he frantically dived to make sure.

Hornicek is nearly embarrassed by Havertz as the Newcastle goalkeeper dawdles on the ball and takes too long to clear. The German forward closes in and blocks Hornicek’s kick, but luckily for the hosts, the ball spins away from goal towards Hall’s feet.

Arsenal go close early on. Eze drifts into a central position and brings down a long ball before teeing up Madueke, who dances inside of Burn and fires a powerful effort against the base of the woodwork. Hornicek seemed to have it covered at his near post, but that was still a notable opening for Arsenal.

Murphy does well to barge past Guimaraes and then attempts a very ambitious lob over Raya from just inside Arsenal’s half. However, the Newcastle man’s hopeful effort skids very far off target. It would take a miracle to beat Raya from that range.

More than £300m worth of signings are on the Newcastle bench this evening and another £72m sitting in the stands. That points to some bungled recruitment decisions over the last 18 months.

The fact that neither Aladji Bamba nor Bazoumane Toure can even make the matchday squad after joining in the summer before Matthias Jaissle was appointed manager is also damning.

There could be some awkward conversations between Jaissle and sporting director Ross Wilson before the January transfer window.

Then again, it was Jaissle who pushed to sign Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City and was thrilled to sign Mathias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille. They cost just over £100m and both only  make the bench against  Arsenal.

St James’ Park is absolutely bouncing. Can Newcastle upset Arsenal’s rhythm and disrupt the runaway leaders’ winning run?

Loud boos and whistles from Newcastle fans when Bruno Guimraes’ name is announced in the Arsenal team and a huge cheer from the away fans.

#964. Preparing for 45C: How Germany tests its crisis response

A record heat wave. Five years of drought. A nation under pressure. Germany is running its biggest joint crisis exercise to date to test how authorities would cope with an escalating climate emergency.

Imagine a situation in which prolonged drought has devastated Germany and much of Europe, taking a toll on people's lives, the environment and economy — with a heat wave with temperatures of up to 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) compounding the situation.

About 180 organizations across Germany, including more than 60 ministries at the state level and nearly 20 federal authorities, are taking part in a major crisis exercise known as LÜKEX 26, which is built around this very scenario.

It is Germany's cross-government crisis management exercise organized by the Federal Office of Civil Protection and Disaster Assistance (BBK). And it's been up and running for more than two decades.

The first LÜKEX in 2004 dealt with the scenario of an extreme winter with a major power outage. Lessons from that exercise proved valuable in 2005 when the Münsterland region of North Rhine-Westphalia — Germany's most populous state — experienced the worst power outage in the country's postwar history. When heavy snowfall caused power lines to collapse, leaving 250,000 people without electricity for days, there was a better understanding of who to contact and where the bottlenecks were.

Since it first started, LÜKEX has trained for scenarios involving terror attacks, an influenza pandemic, biological health threats, storm floods in northern Germany and gas shortages in southern Germany. The most recent exercise in 2023 simulated a cyberattack targeting government operations.

With the help of other ministries, the German Weather Service and the Federal Institute of Hydrology, the BBK developed a drought risk analysis to serve as the scenario.

Participants, which include aid organizations Malteser and the German Red Cross, didn't know the specifics of the challenges they would be facing until the exercise kicked off on Wednesday.

At that point, they were told it was July 20, 2027. In that simulated future, they find themselves in a Germany that has been struggling with extreme heat for weeks; water levels in rivers are falling, food supplies are becoming scarce and emergency services are under growing pressure.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Patrick Pöhler, spokesperson for Malteser, said additional details include supermarkets having run out of water, collapsed supply chains and skyrocketing prices to enter a swimming pool. He said the scenario also goes into how the situation is impacting sections of society.

"Emergency services and elderly care are areas that require particular attention," Pöhler said. "The increasingly extreme summers of recent years have shown how severely heat can affect staffing levels and operational capacity."

In its scenario, the northern port city of Hamburg is tasked with managing the disruption of key transport routes that are impacting access to food and drinking water, as well as handling disinformation attacks that are fueling public fear.

"We have not conducted an exercise of this magnitude since the end of the Cold War. Yet such preparations are essential to strengthen our resilience and crisis-response capabilities," said Hamburg's minister for the interior, Andy Grote.

LÜKEX is designed to test and strengthen the country's ability to manage major crises at a strategic level. No matter the specific scenario, they all help test internal structures, workflows and decision-making processes.

"The lessons learned are continuously incorporated into improving preparedness, planning and cooperation in civil protection," said BBK spokesperson Katharina Böcker.

This year's topic was decided a long time ago, well before recent summers in which Germany experienced extreme heat, she added. Thousands of people died from heat-related causes during the hot months of this year.

"Crises such as extreme heat waves and prolonged droughts can affect large parts of the population and challenge the operational capabilities of our critical structures over an extended period," said Christian Reuter, secretary general of the German Red Cross, another organization taking part.

Observers take note of how organizations react in the crisis scenario to find out what went well and where things didn't run smoothly.

"We are explicitly encouraged to make mistakes," said Malteser's Pöhler, because that is how weaknesses can be identified and addressed.

A first internal debrief is scheduled for Friday, he added.

A preliminary report with the main findings and respective recommendations is due to be published in the first quarter of next year. A full evaluation report will then be released later in the third quarter of 2027.

#961. Tesla to 'wind down' production of flop Cybertruck

Elon Musk's electric pickup for the future will start to be consigned to the past next year. The Cybertruck's bulk and crude shape meant it could only pass regulatory standards in more permissive markets.

Tesla owner Elon Musk said on Friday that the company would scale down production of the Cybertruck at its Austin factory in the coming year.

The South African entrepreneur said Tesla would be scaling back production of his futuristic but often-mocked pickup truck and amping up production of what he hopes will soon become a fleet of fully automated taxis.

"Tesla will be winding down production of the cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production," Musk said on his X social media site.

The announcement follows a bruising week for Musk amid the US midterm elections, where Republicans struggled despite his major donations, with his companies losing billions in value by market capitalization as investors sought to ditch stock.

Musk later responded to a complimentary user online who hailed the Cybertruck as the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made," and calling it an "end of an era" by saying: "True."

For years he had poured much of his enthusiastic marketing zeal into promoting the Cybertruck, saying during the 2023 launch "finally, the future will look like the future."

However the oversized body, straight lines and stainless steel and the post-apocalpytic vibe these created also met with widespread criticism and even mockery.

The electric powertrain was probably a barrier to sales in the US, by far the biggest pickup truck market, where Musk had hoped to take on some of the country's top-selling gas-guzzling vehicles like the Ford F150 or the Chevrolet Silverado and the Dodge Ram.

Meanwhile, the car's striking shape, weight and size made it impossible for Tesla to try to crack Europe, where electric vehicles are gaining a much larger market share.

Unlike in the US, EU safety regulations place considerable emphasis not just on people in cars in accidents, but also on the dangers posed to pedestrians who might be hit by a vehicle. That meant it was not possible for Tesla to register and sell the Cybertruck for road use in Europe.

Beyond this, the vehicle's size would likely have rendered it impractical and unpopular on many European roads, where space tends to be at more of a premium.

Depending how quick the wind-down proves to be, the Cybertruck's production run could prove shorter than its five-year R&D phase.

Given its longstanding issues meeting Musk's very public sales and production predictions, Tesla does not publish sales figures broken down by model.

But according to the automotive data platform Kelley Blue Book, the company sold 20,237 Cybertrucks in the US last year, down from 38,965 in 2024.

At launch in 2023, Musk had predicted unit sales nearer a quarter of a million.

For orientation, Ford sold more than 800,000 F-Series pickups in the US last year, a slight boost on 2024's numbers. These vehicles start at less than half the list price of a Cybertruck in the US.

The IPO for SpaceX this year revealed that Musk's second-largest company was comfortably the biggest buyer of Cybertrucks in 2025. It bought vehicles worth $131 million and did not even enjoy a bulk-buy or friends-rate discount, paying list prices for the fleet.

The Cybercab is a vehicular element in Musk's bid to transform Tesla towards a company focused more on AI and robotics than automobilies.

Rather than just featuring the self-drive or driving assistance programs that Musk has been championing for years, the Cybercab has no steering wheels, pedals or mirrors at all and is designed never to have a human in control.

Musk say the model will be the company's main autonomous model and will supply a global network of Robotaxis.

Starting in the past few months, around 300 such vehicles have been registered and have started operating, on approved roads in the Austin area near Tesla's Gigafactory Texas. They're being added to the existing fleet of autonomous Model Y Teslas being used for the purpose, serving in an area known as a geofence of around 680 square kilometers (264 square miles).

#959. Any regrets, Mauricio? Man Utd are deep in relegation battle after Anfield farce

The Liverpool fans did not miss a beat. They never do. “Poch is at the wheel,” they goaded as this calamity unfolded. But at the wheel of what, a clown car? The look of thunder on Mauricio Pochettino’s face said it all as he got off to the worst start of any Manchester United manager – or head coach – in 100 years.

The Pochettino bandwagon rolled into town with the usual fanfare of a new era, new belief, new hope; and then the wheels came off, the doors collapsed and the engine exploded. The opening quarter of an hour really was that farcical.

In that time, away to Liverpool of all places, they were 2-0 down, a player down – and down and out. If Pochettino had any uncertainty over the scale of the task ahead of him, there it was laid bare. Of course United had some mitigation. They played almost the entire game with 10 men, but teams have coped with that before and shown far more resistance and resilience. By the time United did that, it was game over. No one expected a quick fix, but come on.

Any regrets, Mauricio? Whatever the salary, he could be forgiven for having a few as he watched on. This is a far cry from being in charge of the United States and watching them roll over Haiti 8-0 on aggregate, as he did last week. If Liverpool had been more ruthless, it could have been 8-0 here.

In the end it was 4-0 – the same scoreline by which Lal Hilditch lost his first game at United, away to Bolton Wanderers in October 1926. Hilditch was a stop-gap player-manager and former central defender Pochettino may well have been tempted to bring himself on, even at the age of 54. He could barely have done worse.

Pochettino, too, can take some responsibility. Eyebrows were certainly raised when he dropped Harry Maguire – who he then had to bring on after 22 minutes – to hand Matthijs de Ligt his first Premier League start in 357 days. De Ligt was then at fault for the first and, arguably, the second goal.

Did the head coach start with a back three or a back four? The players seemed confused. It eventually ended up as a back five.

But this was a collective failing for United. From the top – with director of football Jason Wilcox caught on camera with his head buried in his coat – through the club and out on the pitch. Pochettino is big on building a culture. So he has to abolish the comedy and the chaos and restore credibility.

United are deep in a relegation battle. Have no doubt. Eight points after 11 games means they are currently on target for fewer than 28 points, which is a lower points-per-game total than when they were relegated in 1974.

The work needed at United is monumental. The transfer strategy has been inexplicable, with the decision being to rebuild the attack last year, the midfield this summer and wait until next year to remodel the defence. The folly of that has been exposed by the fact that United have conceded 34 goals already this season, the most in the top five European leagues.

United will argue, with justification, that Leny Yoro’s eighth-minute sending-off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity was harsh given that Alexander Isak appeared to have already lost control of the ball. But what was Yoro thinking as he bundled into the back of the forward? And what was De Ligt doing as he watched on, or lumbered on, after failing to track the run from Ronald Araújo’s ball over the top?

Andoni Iraola had a very clear message for his players ahead of this game: don’t fall into a trap.

It’s remarkable to see Manchester United arrive at Anfield in the bottom three but, to go back to that old cliche, the league table will mean nothing when the game begins and Liverpool’s Head Coach knows it only too well.

There will come a point when United leave their desperate form behind and Iraola, who could do with winning this contest after high-profile defeats to Arsenal and Manchester City, Isn’t being kidded by results after 10 games.

“United finished third in the table last season,” Iraola pointed out. “You are looking at a squad with exactly the same players. They had very, very good results, especially in the second half of the season. Now we have just started, this is just 10 games. So, for sure, they will be a lot higher in the table (soon). We have to rate them like this and the truth is the reference we have is that they finished third.”

The key to success for Liverpool will be winning the midfield battle and Dominik Szoboszlai - whose form has been up and down - needs to recapture his best.

It is ironic that in their latest attempt to rejuvenate and restore some of their old fire, Manchester United have turned to a manager whose career needs a similar reawakening.

Having dismissed Michael Carrick so early in the season, United can consider themselves fortunate that a figure of such clout and experience as Mauricio Pochettino was available and willing to leave his role with the United States.

Pochettino can be even more grateful that a club of United’s stature have turned to him in their moment of need.

United need a saviour to first ease them from the relegation zone and then revive their Premier League and Champions League credibility. Pochettino, meanwhile, needed a club like United to save him from a managerial career that promised more than it delivered.

Bruno Fernandes says he has shelved talks over a new contract because it is not the “right moment” for discussions over his future as Manchester United captain.

Fernandes, 32, is out of contract next summer although United have a 12-month option to extend his deal to 2028.

The Portugal midfielder is understood to have rejected two contract offers from United since the summer but said all his focus needs to be on trying to help the team out of their current plight.

United head into Sunday’s game against Liverpool at Anfield second from bottom in the Premier League.

“We spoke about the contract at the end of last season,” Fernandes told Sky Sports.

“We came in at the beginning of this season speaking about the contract, but about the context of the team and the club, I just put that to a side because I don’t think it’s the right moment, neither for me, nor for the club, to be talking about negotiations.

“The most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.”

Fernandes said claims he wants more money or a longer-term deal on offer are incorrect and that if finances were the issue he would have left Old Trafford before now. The captain has previously rejected lucrative offers from Saudi Arabia.

“The club offered me a new contract, so I think that, from their side, shows that they want me to stay,” he said.

“There’s no negotiations ongoing, but I’ve seen people saying that ‘He’s asked for more money, he’s asked for more years’. If I wanted more money, I wouldn’t be here.

“I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester.

“Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had the chance to leave and I always chose to be here.

“The thing is, I’ve always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club. And I always said, in the moment the club thinks it’s time for me to move on, I will move on.

“I’m not going to be the player that I’ve seen many in this time at Manchester United. They’re going to stay here just by staying, just finish my contract and then we will see. In the moment the club says, ‘Bruno, it’s time to part ways’, I’m going to be the first one walking out the door.”

United chief executive Omar Berrada said of Fernandes on Friday that it was “true that we’re having conversations about his new contract” but that the club preferred “to keep that private”.

Having been voted PFA Player of the Year last season, Fernandes’ form has dropped off this term like that of the team.

He was dropped for the 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth in the wake of a 4-1 drubbing by Como when he criticised the tactics and approach of then head coach Michael Carrick.

Mauricio Pochettino, Carrick’s successor, confirmed on Friday that Fernandes would remain as captain.

Fernandes said the United fans had been “far too patient with us” and hopes Pochettino - who wanted to bring the Portuguese to Spurs in 2019 - will bring a fresh energy.

“He’s someone that likes to bring a very good energy to the team, someone very positive, very strong, strict, said it straight away that he won’t allow us to not give him what he demands from the team, from each player,” Fernandes said.

“He wants the club to succeed so much, he wants to win games, and that’s pretty clear and obvious by the way he and his staff speak and want us to improve.

“Obviously [in 2019] I was a very young player that was eager to come to the Premier League. They had [Harry] Kane there, they had Dele Alli, Son, the chance of playing with those players in front was very attractive.”

Mauricio Pochettino has outlined his vision of changing the culture at Manchester United in his attempt to lift the club out of the Premier League relegation zone.

Pochettino arrived in the country on Wednesday after his final matches in charge of the US national team. He has inherited a squad with some players who have publicly criticised their own coach and technical director this season during their slide down the table.

The new United head coach, who has a contract until 2029, mentioned “culture” seven times in his first club interview in a pointed analysis of the work he needs to do at Old Trafford, starting with this weekend’s match against Liverpool at Anfield.

“The culture, to create the culture is the most important,” Pochettino said. “To have the culture is the most important. Create the habit, the principle and I think that is what we want to create. We need to look forward and to find a way to create the best habit and the culture that makes us to be close to win every single game.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of the game everyone has been waiting for as Manchester United prepare to face Liverpool at Anfield in Mauricio Pochettino’s first outing in charge of the club.

Quiet international break at Man Utd? Don’t be ridiculous. Following a dismal start to the season, which has left today’s visitors 19th in the league table with just one win from 10 matches, Michael Carrick was eventually relieved of his duties as head coach and replaced by Pochettino, who left his role as the United States head coach after two years at the helm.

Pochettino has been handed the unenviable task of attempting to rescue Man Utd’s desperate situation in an extremely tumultuous time for the club under the co-ownership of the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Our first game of the Mauricio Pochettino era. Come on United! 🤍🇾🇪 https://t.co/OXEn81kGSF

Speaking in his first press conference as Man Utd boss, Pochettino was asked about creating a culture in a seemingly tricky environment and replied: “We arrived with the idea to create something from scratch, from our own ideas and philosophy in the way that we love to work. I think we find very supportive people in the club that make the adaptation easy, but at the same time, we need to improve our players, like always, you need to improve your players, improve all the ways to create… the way to find a way to perform.

“I think what we need to do is to be very open-minded and try to do our best to try to perform and the players need to buy the idea of we need to improve, and that is our job. After a few days working, the job is to try to find a way to, from Sunday, perform and to start getting the results that the club historically needs, and it’s because Manchester United needs to be in a place, in a different place than we are now.”

Meanwhile, Liverpool are sat in fifth but have only managed one win in five league matches at Anfield this season, meaning they have the third-worst home form in the division. However, Andoni Iraola’s men will move into the top four with three points here and will smell blood against a beleaguered United side.

Kick-off is at 16:30, with team news arriving shortly.

#958. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.
